title: Lula wins Senate backing for fiscal measures after concessions
html:
Government secures 45-31 vote after accepting 25 amendments, preserving the core of its proposed budget adjustment

Atualizado

Brazil’s Senate approved the main provisions of President Lula’s fiscal adjustment package on Thursday (12), backing measures expected to improve public finances by R$45.1 billion to R$56.1 billion in 2027 as the president prepares for his fourth term.

Senators voted 45 to 31 in favor of the bill’s main text after a full day of negotiations in which rapporteur Eduardo Braga, of the Brazilian Democratic Movement (MDB) party in Amazonas state, accepted 25 amendments proposed by fellow lawmakers to secure its passage. At least three contested provisions remain subject to separate votes on Tuesday (17), meaning the Senate has not yet finished considering the legislation.

Among the changes Braga introduced were preserving the current adjustment formula for transfers to the Federal District Constitutional Fund (FCDF) and protecting tax incentives for technology, semiconductors, and vehicles intended for people with disabilities. Members of the economic team believe the changes will not compromise the fiscal impact the government expects, as their effect is estimated at millions rather than billions of reais.

Despite criticism from financial markets, the bill retained authorization to exclude up to R$10.5 billion in diesel subsidies from the 2026 fiscal target calculation, a measure opposed by the Finance Ministry. Although the expenditure is already exempt from the spending limit, it still counts toward the fiscal target. One faction within the government supports the exclusion to avoid deeper spending freezes, including restrictions on congressional earmarks, a position also supported in Congress.

The estimated fiscal impact was also updated. The first version of Braga’s report, presented on Wednesday (11), put the impact at between R$43 billion and R$54 billion. The revised report raised the figures to R$45.1 billion to R$56.1 billion. The change was a correction, as the sum of the individual measures in the previous report already produced the amounts stated in the revised version.

The vote took place amid protests from opposition lawmakers, who argued that the proposal does not deliver genuine fiscal adjustment but instead increases tax revenue and harms businesses, particularly by allowing restrictions on the use of tax credits to offset tax liabilities.

One provision still awaiting a separate vote concerns removing measures that restrict tax offsets, reduce federal transfers to states under the so-called Kandir Law, and prevent the law from creating obligations for the federal government in future fiscal years.

Lawmakers have also requested a separate vote on an amendment proposed by Senator Rogério Marinho, of the Liberal Party in Rio Grande do Norte state. His proposal would lower the spending threshold that triggers budget freezes from 2% to 0.6%, expand the scope for expenditure restraint, and eliminate the provision that allows diesel subsidies to be excluded from the calculation of the 2026 primary fiscal target. Marinho also proposes removing changes to transfers under the Kandir Law and deleting the article dealing with pension-related financial compensation. The Kandir Law is a tax statute that exempts exported goods and services from the state-level value-added tax.

Opposition lawmakers argue that the bill is designed to give the government room to add new spending to the 2027 budget, including earmarks allocated by congressional committees. Those earmarks are not included in the R$44.8 billion set aside for mandatory congressional earmarks in the executive branch’s budget proposal. Committee earmarks were excluded because they are not mandatory. The law sets a ceiling on their value but does not require their inclusion in the budget.

Speaking on the Senate floor, Marinho described the proposal as budgetary sleight of hand and a kind of deception.

“The public is being told that fiscal adjustment is being carried out, but there is no fiscal adjustment here at all,” he said.

Most of the projected fiscal improvement will come from a combination of spending restraint and increased revenue. The government estimates savings of R$12.8 billion to R$18.3 billion from budget freezes aimed at achieving the midpoint of the fiscal target, along with an equivalent revenue gain from restrictions on tax offsets. Another R$15 billion is expected from reductions in tax incentives, plus R$4.5 billion from limiting a tax benefit to its 2026 value, adjusted for inflation.

One of Braga’s main concessions during the negotiations was the preservation of the Federal District Constitutional Fund. The revised report explicitly states that transfers to the fund will continue to be adjusted according to changes in the federal government’s net current revenue, including in 2027. This protects the fund from the bill’s restrictions on the growth of certain expenditures linked to federal revenue, preserving its existing funding adjustment formula.

On taxation, the rapporteur also expanded the exceptions to cuts in tax incentives. He preserved benefits linked to industrial policy for the information and communications technology and semiconductor sectors, as well as federal incentives for people with disabilities or autism spectrum disorder to purchase vehicles.

Braga also exempted the Social Security Contribution on Gross Revenue, a regime associated with payroll tax relief, from the tax-benefit reduction. According to the economic team, the fiscal impact of the additional exceptions is not significant.

Another change narrows the scope of budget-freezing mechanisms. The revised text explicitly protects debt-service expenditures, innovation and scientific and technological development financed by a dedicated fund, and spending exempted under the Budget Guidelines Act. Braga also established that any permanent reduction or cancellation of these budget allocations would require authorization in the annual budget law.

The senator also limited the government’s authority to restrict tax offsets. Under the revised wording, the measure may apply to the use of credits arising from other taxes administered by the federal tax authority to settle tax liabilities. According to members of the economic team, the change merely restored the proposal’s original wording after an error in the previous report.

Braga also changed the rules governing the use of savings that could result from regulations addressing public-sector pay above the constitutional ceiling.

Under the previous version, the bill would have allowed part of the spending limits assigned to other branches of government and autonomous institutions to be transferred to the executive branch to finance investments and activities related to public security and services for young offenders.

The revised text prohibits such transfers and requires any savings those institutions achieve to remain within their own budgets. It also bars transferring those resources and reducing spending limits for other branches and autonomous institutions, including changes that would affect subsequent fiscal years.

The bill retains a requirement for Congress to consider, within 120 days of the law’s publication, a proposal regulating a constitutional provision concerning public-sector compensation.

Braga also added investments proposed by state congressional delegations to the categories of expenditure eligible for additional funding in the following year if the government achieves a fiscal result above the lower limit of its target range. The measure is conditional on implementation of the spending-restraint measures provided for in the bill.

Another change removed a provision that would have allowed the executive branch to redirect up to 40% of the accumulated financial surplus from certain earmarked funding sources.

According to members of the economic team, removing the provision does not affect the spending-restraint effort because it was meant to increase budget flexibility and prevent the government from having to borrow to finance expenditures.

The revised bill also eliminated a requirement for the Budget Guidelines Law to include a plan to gradually bring the growth of mandatory expenditures closer to the spending growth limit established by Brazil’s fiscal framework.

The provision would have required regulatory and administrative measures, including efforts to combat fraud and irregularities, to contain the growth of those expenditures over five fiscal years.

The main fiscal adjustment mechanisms were preserved, including the option to limit real growth in federal expenditures to 2%, below the 2.5% ceiling established by the fiscal framework. The restriction could be applied from 2027 onward in years when the spending-restraint measures provided for in the bill are triggered, without permanently changing the baseline used to calculate expenditures.

The revised report also retains authorization for the government to freeze budget allocations even when the projected primary fiscal balance remains within the lower tolerance band of the fiscal target.

summary: The upper house approved the main text of an adjustment worth up to about 60 billion reais.
